title: HaloAI - POC capacity & autoscale scoping
summary: POC scoping for capacity sizing and autoscaling. Discussed workload profile (batch vs interactive), target p95/p50 latency, reserved GPU commit, burst strategy, fallback to quantized smaller model, KV prefix/cache considerations, benchmark plan and 2-week pilot timeline. Agreed next steps: share benchmark harness, initial capacity proposal, security docs, and schedule benchmark run next Tuesday.

transcript:
Header: 2026-10-05 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~58m | Attendees: Jordan Price (Redwood AE), Sana Malik (Redwood SE), Priya Shah (HaloAI), Liam O'Connell (Halo Infra), Marcus Reed (Halo Product)

[00:00] Jordan: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Jordan from Redwood, AE on this account. Sana from our infra and serving team is with me. How's everyone doing?
[00:17] Priya: Good thanks. Excited to dig into the POC sizing — we want to make sure we don't overprovision but still hit latency goals.
[00:28] Marcus: Yeah quick context, we're building a semi-real time summarization and search assistant for enterprise docs. Peak concurrency right now is about, um, 180 concurrent user requests during business hours, roughly 2K unique requests per minute at peak.
[00:45] Liam: Our current stack is on GCP, using GKE with node pools for GPUs. We also have on-prem infra for sensitive data that we may want to route to during pilot.
[01:02] Jordan: Great. Quick assumptive read: model family you're testing? Priya?
[01:09] Priya: We're looking at a 13B dense model fine-tuned for summarization, but we also have a 70B variant we might fallback to for higher quality in some flows. Mostly 13B for latency.
[01:21] Sana: Perfect. For POC scoping we'll need: sample traces, desired SLOs (p50/p95 latency), sequence length distributions, and any hot-path prompts. Also curious about concurrency distribution — steady vs spiky.
[01:38] Priya: Average sequence length is 512 tokens, but summaries can go up to 1,024 tokens. P50 is about 350. SLO target p95 is <= 800ms for interactive calls, p50 we'd like under 300ms.
[01:54] Jordan: Okay noted. On the capacity side, we typically recommend reserved baseline GPUs to cover steady-state, with a burst pool to handle spikes. For a 13B model on Nvidia A100-ish hardware, a rough thumb is 12-18 concurrent inferences per GPU depending on batching and context length.
[02:14] Liam: Wait that 12-18 number — is that with kv cache warm? And is that per A100 40GB or 80GB?
[02:22] Sana: Good question. The numbers vary; for A100 80GB with q4 quant or fp16 that's with KV cache effective and continuous batching. Cold starts and long contexts reduce throughput. For 512 tokens p50 we see, um, about 15 concurrent per A100; for 1024 tokens it drops to 8-9.
[02:45] Priya: So for our 180 concurrent users what are we looking at for reserved GPUs?
[02:51] Sana: If your steady concurrency is 180 and average concurrency per GPU is, say, 12 (conservative), you'd need 15 GPUs reserved to cover steady-state. But that's heavy; for POC we usually suggest reserving a smaller baseline — e.g., 6 GPUs — and configure autoscale to burst to 18. That plus fallback policies.
[03:14] Marcus: Hmm 6 baseline feels light. What's the logic?
[03:18] Jordan: Baseline covers typical daily load and keeps cost predictable. Burst handles peak traffic; autoscaling can spin up more nodes, though there is a warmup time. We also recommend a fallback policy: when capacity constrained, route to a quantized 7B variant (or Redwood-hosted low-latency variant) with similar prompt engineering to maintain UX while you scale.
[03:37] Priya: How long is the warmup for burst? If we get a 2x spike that'll push p95 past 1.5s if warmup takes a minute.
[03:46] Sana: Warmup depends on whether the nodes are pre-warmed with model artifacts. Cold provisioning from zero can take 1-3 minutes for large models. We can use a burst pool with pre-loaded containers (keeps GPUs warm but costs more). Another pattern is predictive warmup: use historical signals to spin up in advance for known peak windows.
[04:05] Liam: For security reasons we need the POC to run inside our VPC for some test flows. Can Redwood Dedicated do that or is that Redwood Private?
[04:14] Jordan: Redwood Dedicated provides dedicated GPU pools with network isolation but still managed control plane; Redwood Private is the customer-managed control plane option for fully private deployments. For the pilot, Dedicated with VPC peering usually suffices. We'll share the network checklist.
[04:29] Liam: Cool, we'll need SAML SSO for console access and KMS integration for keys.
[04:36] Jordan: Yep we support SSO, RBAC, and KMS/HSM integrations. We'll attach SOC2 and audit log docs in the follow up.
[04:47] Marcus: Back to benchmarks — what's the plan? We want meaningful numbers matching our prod traffic.
[04:53] Sana: Two-pronged: synthetic microbenchmarks to measure per-GPU throughput and p95/p50 at different sequence lengths, then replay-based testing using your traffic trace to measure end-to-end latencies and autoscale behavior. We'll run both on your target model(s) with the same prompts.
[05:10] Priya: If we replay traffic, can you simulate burst patterns? We have daily spikes that are predictable.
[05:16] Sana: Yes we can use the harness to re-create spikes, traffic ramps, and steady-state. We'll capture token generation rates, p50/p95/p99, and GPU utilization. We'll also test fallback policies — like automatic fallback to a quantized 7B if p95 crosses threshold, or route to Hosted API as backstop.
[05:34] Liam: What about batching and latency tradeoffs? We can't batch too aggressively or interactive latency suffers.
[05:40] Sana: Agreed. We'll tune batching profiles per route: tight latency SLO routes get small batch size and prefer prefetched KV caching; throughput routes can tolerate larger batch sizes. Our runtime supports continuous batching and dynamic batch sizing.
[05:54] Priya: Can you give an example capacity table? Like baseline GPUs vs burst threshold vs fallback threshold?
[06:00] Jordan: Sure, example for your profile: baseline reserve 6 A100-80GB; autoscale policy to add +3 GPUs per scale event up to max 18. Burst pre-warm of 4 GPUs for predictable windows. Fallback rules: if queue delay > 400ms or p95 > 900ms for 2 consecutive minutes, begin routing 30% of traffic to the quantized 7B model, and if still degraded, route to Hosted low-latency model.
[06:26] Marcus: That routing split — can it be per-route? We have search versus summarization endpoints.
[06:31] Sana: Yes, routing is per-route. You can set different SLOs and fallback policies per route.
[06:36] Priya: For the POC we want to test both: route A (summarization) needs stricter quality, route B (search snippets) can tolerate smaller models.
[06:45] Jordan: Makes sense. For the POC we'll propose: 1) baseline 6 GPUs 2) autoscale to 18, 3) pre-warm 4 GPUs during business peak windows, 4) fallback quantized 7B for search route only, and 5) measure end-to-end p95 and regression in quality for fallback.
[07:05] Liam: How do we measure quality regressions when falling back? We need a small eval set and automatic quality alerts.
[07:11] Sana: We suggest a holdout prompt set (50-200 examples) and a simple metric like ROUGE or embed-sim cosine similarity to the reference; Redwood Optimize can run regression alerts against that set and trigger downstream alerts.
[07:25] Priya: We'll prepare a 100-prompt eval set.
[07:28] Jordan: Great. Timeline — how long for the POC?
[07:31] Sana: Typical POC is 2 weeks: week 1 environment setup + synthetic microbenchmarks + connect VPC; week 2 run replay benchmarks, validate autoscale and fallback, analyze results and present findings. If you want a longer soak we can extend.
[07:45] Marcus: That works. When can we start?
[07:48] Jordan: If you can share traces and access this week, we can start setup next Monday and aim to run benchmarks mid-week (week of 2026-10-12).
[07:56] Priya: We'll share traces by Friday.
[07:59] Liam: On the technical details, how does KV/prefix cache affect memory and throughput? We have long contexts and repeated doc prefixes.
[08:07] Sana: KV cache helps a lot for multi-turn or repeated-prefix workloads by avoiding re-compute. It increases memory usage (KV storage on GPU RAM) but reduces per-token compute. For your 512-1024 token contexts, storing prefix caches for hot-docs will improve p95 substantially. We'll also recommend model sharding configs if using very large models.
[08:27] Priya: Any gotchas with quantization? We care about quality drop when moving to q4 or int8.
[08:33] Sana: There is a measurable quality drop; we'll quantify it on your eval set. For some summaries q4 works fine, for others you need 13B fp16. The fallback can be dynamic: send the short/low-complexity prompts to quantized model, high-complexity to baseline.
[08:53] Marcus: For cost, how do we meter the burst usage vs reserved?
[08:58] Jordan: Reserved is commitment pricing; burst is pay-as-you-go at a higher per-hour rate. We'll include a cost projection with both steady-state and burst scenarios in the capacity proposal.
[09:09] Priya: Good. A few clarifying Qs — if autoscale can't spin up more GPUs due to quota, do you have capacity pool fallbacks?
[09:17] Sana: We do. Smart routing can fallback to other regions or to smaller model variants, and there's an emergency route to Redwood Hosted API to maintain availability. We'll simulate quota failure in the replay tests.
[09:28] Liam: Can the POC include on-prem path for sensitive traffic? We want to verify latency inside our DC.
[09:34] Jordan: Yes, we can run a hybrid. Some traffic can be routed to private on-prem nodes (if you allow agent install) while the rest goes to Dedicated. For POC we'll prototype with VPC + peering first.
[09:47] Priya: Ok, action items recap?
[09:50] Jordan: I'll capture: send capacity + pricing proposal, share network checklist, Sana will set up benchmark harness, Priya will share traces and eval set, Liam will do firewall/VPC checks.
[09:58] Marcus: Sounds good. Anything else?
[10:00] Priya: Please add an explicit measurement for warmup time in the benchmark results and capture p95 over the warmup window.
[10:06] Sana: Will do. We'll instrument timestamps for when nodes are allocated, model load time, and p95 during ramp.
[10:12] Jordan: Perfect. We'll follow up with an email with the docs and proposed schedule. Thanks everyone.
[10:19] Priya: Thanks all.
[10:21] Marcus: Thanks.
[10:23] Liam: Bye.
